builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
summary: The workflow replaces one-time, release-and-freeze benchmark curation with continuous validation combining community reports, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs, plus explicit validation of resource budgets such as wall-clock limits. It costs ongoing human review effort, re-running of evaluations after repairs, and added infrastructure for trace collection and oracle checks, all feasible on a single GPU or via APIs since only agents are executed, not trained. It can fail if human gating becomes a bottleneck, if repairs are inconsistent or introduce new verifier biases, or if revalidated resource settings are not reported, making scores incomparable across evaluations.
rationale: Any team deploying coding agents in production relies on benchmark scores for model selection, and this paper shows stale benchmarks misstate accuracy by over 10 points, so adopting continuous validation and explicit resource-budget reporting directly improves procurement and evaluation decisions at low infrastructure cost.
technique: Continuous benchmark validation and repair workflow

claims.statement: The workflow replaces one-time, release-and-freeze benchmark curation with continuous validation combining community reports, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs, plus explicit validation of resource budgets such as wall-clock limits. It costs ongoing human review effort, re-running of evaluations after repairs, and added infrastructure for trace collection and oracle checks, all feasible on a single GPU or via APIs since only agents are executed, not trained. It can fail if human gating becomes a bottleneck, if repairs are inconsistent or introduce new verifier biases, or if revalidated resource settings are not reported, making scores incomparable across evaluations.

Repairs to Terminal-Bench 2.0 (issues in ~30% of tasks) raised measured accuracy by over 10 percentage points and shifted leaderboard positions by up to three ranks (Spearman rho = 0.958); extending wall-clock limits closed a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrank a 30pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5pp.
